prompt: Explain what an API is to a non-technical client.

task.prompt: Explain it in plain words, with no jargon.
task.context: Client: "The developers keep saying the app talks to an API. What is that?"

rubric.label: Correct
rubric.description: An API is how two systems ask each other for data or actions.

rubric.label: Plain language
rubric.description: No jargon; an everyday comparison is welcome.

task.sampleAnswer: An API is like a waiter: your app sends a request to another system and brings back the answer, like prices or payments.

prompt: A PM drafted this update for a non-technical client. Mark the lines the client won't understand.

task.prompt: Mark every segment that is a problem. Leave the sound ones unmarked.

segments.text: Hi Maria, here's this week's update.
The login screen is finished and ready for you to try.
We refactored the monolith and fixed the N+1 queries in the ORM.
segments.issue: Jargon with no meaning for the client; say what they get: faster pages.

segments.text: Search results now load in under a second.
Next we'll bump the SDK and resolve merge conflicts on main.
segments.issue: Internal detail the client cannot use; describe the outcome instead.

segments.text: Please test the login before Thursday's call.

prompt: Explain staging versus production to a non-technical client.

task.prompt: Explain the difference simply and why it matters to them.
task.context: Client: "Why can I see the new feature on one link but not in the real app?"

rubric.label: Correct
rubric.description: Staging is a private test copy; production is the live app real users see.

rubric.label: Why it matters
rubric.description: Testing in staging protects real users.

task.sampleAnswer: Staging is a private copy for testing; production is the live app. We check features on staging first so real users never hit bugs.

prompt: Explain DNS propagation to a non-technical client.

task.prompt: Explain why their new domain isn't working everywhere yet.
task.context: Client: "We switched the domain an hour ago. It works for me but not for my colleague. Is it broken?"

rubric.label: Correct
rubric.description: Address updates spread across the internet gradually; old copies expire over hours.

rubric.label: Reassuring and timed
rubric.description: Not broken; usually up to 24-48 hours.

task.sampleAnswer: It isn't broken. The internet's address books update gradually, so some people see the new site sooner. It usually settles within 48 hours.

prompt: After a release, the client says they still see the old version of the website.

task.prompt: Choose the best option at each step.

steps.question: What is the most likely plain-language explanation?
options: The release failed and must be redone.
Their browser or a cache is still showing a saved copy of the old pages.
The developers released to the wrong client.
Their internet is too slow.
steps.explanation: Caches keep copies of pages to load them faster, so old versions can linger briefly after a release.

steps.question: What do you ask them to try first?
options: Reinstall their browser.
A hard refresh or a private window, then tell you what they see.
Wait a month.
Buy a new domain.
steps.explanation: A hard refresh or private window bypasses the saved copy and quickly shows whether the release is live.

prompt: Explain technical debt to a non-technical client.

task.prompt: Explain what it is and why you are asking for time to fix it.
task.context: You want one sprint to clean up rushed code from the launch. Client: "Why pay for work that adds no features?"

rubric.label: Correct
rubric.description: Shortcuts taken to ship faster that make later changes slower and riskier.

rubric.label: Business value
rubric.description: Fixing it makes future features faster and safer.

rubric.label: Plain language
rubric.description: No jargon; an analogy is fine.

task.sampleAnswer: To launch fast we took shortcuts. Like an unpaid loan, they slow every new feature. One sprint now makes future work faster and safer.

prompt: Put the steps in order: how a developer's change reaches the client's users.

task.prompt: Drag the items into the right order, first at the top.

items.label: Developer writes the change on a separate branch
Change is deployed to staging for testing
Pull request is opened and reviewed by another developer

task.explanation: Code is reviewed and tested automatically, checked on staging, and only then released to real users.

prompt: A client wants an AI chatbot on their website that answers customers' questions about their refund policy.

task.prompt: Choose the best option at each step.

steps.question: How do you explain the main risk in plain language?
options: AI is always right, so there's no risk.
It can sound confident but give a wrong answer, such as an incorrect refund rule.
AI chatbots don't work on websites.
It will read all their private emails.
steps.explanation: LLMs can 'hallucinate': produce fluent but wrong answers. For policies that matters.

steps.question: Which mitigation do you suggest?
options: Ground answers in their actual policy pages, show the source, and hand off to a person when unsure.
Let it answer anything with no checks.
Never launch any AI feature.
Ask customers to double-check with Google.
steps.explanation: Grounding in real documents, citing sources and a human fallback reduce wrong answers.

prompt: In plain language, what does an SSL certificate do for a website?

options: Makes the website load faster
Encrypts the connection and shows the padlock in the browser
Backs up the website every night
Blocks all spam emails
mcq.explanation: SSL/TLS encrypts data between visitor and site; browsers show a padlock and warn when it is missing or expired.

prompt: A developer says, "the bug is in the backend." What does that mean for the client?

options: The problem is in the server side that stores and processes data, not the screens
The bug is at the bottom of the page
The bug is on the client's own computer
The bug is in the design files
mcq.explanation: The backend is the server-side logic and data; the frontend is what users see and tap.

prompt: What does CI/CD mean, in plain language?

options: A type of database
Code changes are automatically tested and released in small, frequent steps
A contract clause about delivery dates
The client signs off every line of code
mcq.explanation: Continuous integration and delivery: automatic tests on every change and a repeatable release process.

prompt: A client asks what an AI "hallucination" is. Which answer is accurate?

options: The AI is overheating
The AI gives a fluent, confident answer that is wrong or made up
The AI refuses to answer
The AI shows images instead of text
mcq.explanation: Hallucinations are plausible-sounding but false outputs, which is why AI answers need grounding and checks.
